newsitem.title: USA: Centennial to restate losses to 1994, stock plunges.
newsitem.headline: Centennial to restate losses to 1994, stock plunges.

text.p: The stock of Centennial Technologies Inc. lost three-quarters of its value Thursday after the company said it would restate its earnings to show a loss for the last 3-1/2 years rather than a profit.
The stock was halted all day Wednesday pending the news.

The small manufacturer of personal computer memory cards, whose founder and fired Chief Executive Emanuel Pinez sits in jail on charges of insider trading, had reported earnings totalling $12.1 million over the last 3-1/2 fiscal years.

The news sent its shares plunging on the New York Stock Exchange just two days after they more than tripled on news the company had record sales last week. The exchange said on Monday that it will delist the company.

Centennial -- the best performing stock on the New York Stock Exchange last year -- lost three-quarters of its value, falling $11.25 to $3.50. It was the most active issue on the NYSE in afternoon trading.
Centennial said it was continuing its financial review, with the help of two teams of outside auditors, and its investigation into "certain activities" when Pinez was chief executive.

Pinez was charged by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the U.S. Attorney's office in Boston earlier this month with insider trading and with inflating sales figures. He was denied bail last week and has been held in a Plymouth, Mass. jail.
Pinez has denied, through his lawyer, any wrongdoing.
The restated earnings for the last 3-1/2 years will be released in about six to 12 weeks, the company said.

"The anticipated restatements will relate both to the company's operations, including an inventory write-off and sales reversals, and to non-operating losses attributable to an anticipated write-down of the carrying value of certain investments," the company said in a short statement.
Officials with the company declined to elaborate.
Billerica, Mass.-based Centennial said just last week that it would have to restate its earnings for the last 18 months to show a loss instead of profits of $10.8 million.
In 1996, Centennial's stock rose more than fivefold, but it has been on a rocky ride since. Beginning the year at $55, the stock plummetted to a low of $1.75 last week.
"In a period of 60 days when you see a stock go from $55 to $2, that ranks right up there with any of them," said the president of a brokerage who has been in the business for more than 40 years.
Some brokers who followed Centennial were surprised the New York Stock Exchange resumed trade, given that it would be delisted on Monday anyway.

"If you were a holder and you wanted to sell, you would want that opportunity," said Ray Pellecchia, a spokesman for the NYSE. The NYSE also gave the company about two weeks to find another exchange for the stock in accordance with standard procedures, he said.

Centennial's interim Chief Executive Lawrence Ramaekers said in an interview on Tuesday that the company would not seek another stock exchange listing until it had more complete financial information available.

The brokerage president, who declined to be identified, said questions will arise over how Pinez hid his alleged falsifications from the company's board of directors, its auditors and regulators for so long.
"I'm sure there will be a heck of a lot of finger-pointing," he said.
He said Centennial's legal difficulties, including a slew of shareholder lawsuits, may make it impossible to operate the company.
